where: the reserved reply line under "Check again" and the Project / Service account list beneath it
finding: The reply slot reserves more height than its line uses, and the surplus falls out of the bottom of the group. The result is that the fact list is separated from the section it belongs to by very slightly more space than separates the whole section from the next one. "This deployment" now reads as heading, verdict, caveat, control, reply — and then a second, unlabelled block of two identifiers that could belong to either neighbour. The reader has to decide for themselves which heading the project and service account answer to, and the only answer the layout offers is the wrong one.
evidence: Setup fold: the "Checked 6:41 pm" line ends at y=610 and "Project" starts at y=642 — 31px — while the fact list ends at y=712 and the next section's heading starts at y=742, 29px. Two gaps the eye cannot tell apart, one of them internal. The same slack repeats in the denied frame, where the reply sits under the two command buttons.
direction: Reserve the reply's growth inside the group rather than letting it trail off the group's bottom edge, and set the section's internal gaps so that no gap inside a section is as large as the gap between sections. The facts should be visibly the tail of the block whose heading they sit under.

finding: The panel hangs its fill and ring outside the text column so its first character sits on the page's left edge — a good move at the desktop's wide gutter, but the phone column is inset far less, so the same outdent leaves the panel a hair's breadth from the screen edge while every other block on the page starts on the column. It is neither aligned nor bled: a near-miss margin reads as a slip rather than as a decision, and it is the only object on the denied page that breaks the page's left edge.
evidence: Denied fold: the panel's ring begins 3px from the viewport edge, against the 16px inset that the h1, the danger sentence, the field, the button and every heading below the rule share. At a glance the code block looks like it has escaped the layout rather than been placed outside it.
direction: Let the hang be sized to the gutter it hangs into: on the phone either put the panel back on the column with the field and the button, or take it fully to the screen edge as an honest bleed. The choice should be legible as a choice at both widths, which a 3px margin is not.

where: the resting pairing field and its six placeholder marks
finding: The field became the lit surface it was asked to be, but its contents did not come up with it. The value of the placeholder was raised; its scale was not. Six 3px dots sit in the middle of a 358x60 surface, occupying about a third of its width and a fifteenth of its height, so the object that arrives at a squint is a large empty tray rather than six waiting slots. The one thing the field could say without being read — that it wants six characters, in the shape they will land in — it does not say; that job is left entirely to the label above it. The composition is now correct in rank and still mute in content.
evidence: Setup fold: the placeholder marks measure 3px wide against the 30px monospace that will replace them, and the cluster spans 122px of a 358px box. Its centre also sits about 3px left of the box's centre, because the trailing letter-space of the tracking is being counted into the centring — visible as slightly more air to the right of the last dot than to the left of the first.
direction: Let the resting field show the shape of its answer at the scale of the type that will fill it — marks weighted to the glyphs they stand in for, or six positions marked by the surface itself — and centre what the reader sees rather than the string plus its trailing space.

where: the foot of the page, from the "Check in" link down
finding: The page fits the viewport with room to spare and then trails off. Its last three moves are the one way onward, a rule, and two paragraphs of the faintest small print on the screen — after which a fifth of the frame is empty. So the composition ends on its least important material and the blank below is left over rather than used. On a screen that holds exactly two things, the closing note should be the one the reader might act on; here the reference prose gets the last word and then nothing does.
evidence: Counselor fold: content stops at y=665 of an 844px frame, with 180px of unbroken page beneath the retirement paragraph. "Check in" — the page's only remaining action — sits at y=438, above both footnotes.
direction: Decide what closes the page and let the order say it. Either the reference paragraphs move above the exit so the action is the last thing the composition offers, or the exit takes the foot of the frame and the emptiness sits between the two registers instead of after them. The blank should be a margin the layout chose, not the space the content ran out in.

where: the bottom sheet: the identity block against the single destination row
finding: The header now outweighs the list it introduces. On the admin build the identity block and three destination rows balance; with a counselor's one row, the same header is twice the height of the list, carries four text objects to the list's one, and holds the panel's only chroma. The surface therefore reads as an account card with a link stapled underneath, and the first thing it presents is the red exit rather than the one place it exists to offer. The proportion tells the reader the account is the subject; it is not.
evidence: Counselor menu fold: the identity block runs about 99px, the destination list one 48px row reading "Kiosk". Squinting the panel, "Sign out" arrives, then the email, then the single destination last.
direction: Let the header scale with the list it introduces — the role is a fact about the email and does not need a line to itself, which would also stop the exit needing a line of its own — or let a sole destination carry the presence a panel's subject deserves. In a navigation surface the destinations should arrive before the account they belong to, whatever their number.
